passage:
Monday: Rekha dropped an easy catch at cricket practice. Walking off, she muttered to Charu, 'I ruin everything. I'm useless at all of it.' That night she didn't open her maths homework. What was the point?
Wednesday: the maths test came back with a C. 'See? I'm dumb at everything,' Rekha said at the water cooler. Charu frowned. 'You got a B last month. And you didn't do Monday's homework.' That evening Rekha wrote 'Things I'm bad at' in her rough book: catching, maths, speaking in class. Writing it down felt honest, like facing facts.
Saturday: the science club was building its water rocket at ten. Rekha had been excited about it for a month. At nine she messaged Charu: 'Not going. I'll just mess it up like everything else.' Charu replied, 'You designed the fins!' Rekha put the phone face down on the bed and stared at the ceiling fan.

qa.q: What happened to Rekha at cricket practice on Monday?
qa.a: Rekha dropped an easy catch at cricket practice.

qa.q: Why did writing the 'Things I'm bad at' list feel honest to Rekha?
qa.a: She felt defeated and believed one dropped catch and one C proved she was bad at everything, so the list seemed like plain facts rather than a gloomy habit.

qa.q: Where was the turning point for Rekha, and what could she have done?
qa.a: On Saturday she could have gone to the rocket build anyway, testing her belief against the fact that she designed the fins.

qa.q: How might Charu feel reading 'Not going'?
qa.a: Charu probably felt frustrated and worried, because Charu could see Rekha giving up on something Rekha had been excited about for a month.

grounding: A teenage girl treats one setback as proof she fails at everything, skips homework and a science-club build, while treating this as facing facts.

passage: Trisha, you think I was always this cheerful old man? At sixteen your Ojas Dadu was the gloomiest boy in Nagpur. When I failed the chemistry practical, I told myself, you are finished, you are a fool at everything. And I believed it completely. The drawing competition that month, I didn't enter. The school cricket selection, I didn't go. My friends said, 'Arre, it was one practical.' I said, 'You don't understand, I'm just being honest about myself.' It felt like honesty. It felt grown up. Only much later I noticed that my father spoke the same way. When his scooter broke, it was 'our family never has luck'. When it rained on a holiday, 'this always happens to us'. I had learned that voice like I learned his walk. So when you say, 'I'm bad at everything', beti, I listen carefully. Whose voice is that?

qa.q: What did Ojas Dadu fail at sixteen?
qa.a: He failed the chemistry practical.

qa.q: What did young Ojas believe after failing, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt hopeless, believing he was finished and a fool at everything, which shows in how he skipped both the drawing competition and the cricket selection.

qa.q: What could Trisha do the next time she hears herself say 'I'm bad at everything'?
qa.a: She could stop and ask whose voice that is, as Dadu suggests, and look at the one real setback instead of giving up on everything.

qa.q: How might Ojas's friends have seen him skipping the drawing competition and cricket selection?
qa.a: They probably saw a boy giving up on things he could do because of one failed practical, which is why they said it was only one practical.

grounding: A grandfather tells his granddaughter how, as a teenager, he saw one failure as proof he was bad at everything and gave up, a habit he later realised he had learned from his father.

passage: The monsoon arrived a day early on the school camp near Lonavala. At four in the afternoon, Ganga's tent sagged and collapsed in the rain, soaking her sleeping bag. The others shrieked and laughed and ran for the dining shed. Ganga stood in the mud. 'Of course,' she said. 'I mess up everything. Even tents.' Farhan held up a snapped pole. 'Ganga, this was broken. Nobody could have kept it up.' She didn't look at it. 'It's always me. I'll be useless on the trek tomorrow too. I'm staying back.' 'It's the easy trail,' Farhan said. 'You'll slow everyone down.' At dinner she ate quietly, already sure. In the morning, when the teacher called names for the trek, Ganga said she had a headache. Farhan watched her from the gate as the group left without her.

qa.q: What did Farhan hold up after the tent collapsed?
qa.a: Farhan held up a snapped pole.

qa.q: Why didn't Ganga look at the broken pole Farhan held up?
qa.a: She felt defeated and already sure the fault was hers and always would be, so she didn't want evidence that pointed to something else.

qa.q: What choice could Ganga have made in the morning?
qa.a: She could have gone on the easy trail and seen how the trek actually went, instead of saying she had a headache and staying back.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel watching the group leave without Ganga?
qa.a: Farhan may feel sad and a bit helpless, since Farhan tried to show her the pole was broken and she still gave up.

grounding: A teenage girl blames herself for a tent failure caused by a broken pole, decides she'll fail at the trek too and gives up without trying.

passage: In the school auditorium in Chandigarh, the Class 10 play rehearsal stopped dead. Baljeet had forgotten the second line of the big speech, again. Ma'am said, "Take it from the top." Baljeet shook his head, face hot. On the bench outside afterwards he told Payal, "I'm quitting. And the debate team. I mess up everything I touch." "It's one line," Payal said. "It's not one line. It's me. It's always been me." He said it calmly, like reading out a weather report. "I'm not being dramatic. I'm just being realistic." Payal remembered him saying the same in Class 8 about football, and then chess. Each time he had quit within a week. "Realistic would be: you learnt that whole speech in four days," she said. Baljeet shrugged and walked to the bus stop, the script still in his hand.

qa.q: Which two things did Baljeet say he was quitting?
qa.a: The play and the debate team.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet believe he was being realistic?
qa.a: He saw one forgotten line as proof of a permanent flaw that spoils everything, so the gloomy view felt like plain fact to him.

qa.q: At this turning point, what could Baljeet try instead of quitting?
qa.a: He could treat it as one line that needs practice, not a verdict on himself, and run the speech a few more times before deciding anything.

qa.q: How does Payal see Baljeet's 'realism'?
qa.a: Payal sees a pattern of football, chess and now the play, each dropped within a week, and thinks the real facts, like learning the speech in four days, point the other way.

grounding: A teenager treats one forgotten line as proof he ruins everything, calls it realism, and moves to give up quickly.

passage:
"Navneet, coach wants us back for extra practice on Friday."
"I'm not coming, Thomas. I'm done with football."
"Because of one penalty?"
"Because I'm the kind of person who misses penalties. And fails chemistry. And forgot Mum's birthday. It's everything."
"You forgot her birthday?"
"Last year. See? It's a pattern."
"Okay, but you scored twice in the semi."
"Luck."
"So the miss is you, and the goals are luck?"
"That's just how it works for me."
"That's a weird rule."
"It's not a rule. It's the truth. I'm being honest."
"Come Friday anyway. Take five penalties. If you miss all five, fine, I'll stop asking."
"...I'll think about it."

qa.q: How many goals did Navneet score in the semi?
qa.a: Navneet scored twice in the semi.

qa.q: Why does Navneet believe the miss is personal but the goals are luck?
qa.a: Navneet feels hopeless and discouraged, treating setbacks as personal and permanent while explaining successes away, and this feels like honesty rather than a habit.

qa.q: What choice does Thomas offer at the turning point, and why could it help?
qa.a: Five penalties on Friday: a small test that could give Navneet real evidence instead of the gloomy story.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Navneet's 'rule'?
qa.a: Thomas finds it strange that the goals don't count, and seems to see a teammate talking their way out of something they are good at.

grounding: A teenager treats one missed penalty as proof of failing at everything, dismisses successes as luck, and calls the pessimism honesty.

passage:
"I'm not going for the debate trials either."
"Chandrika, you didn't make the basketball team. What's debate got to do with it?"
"Everything. I'm just not good enough, Devika didi. Not at basketball, not at debate, not at anything. That's how I am."
"You were picked last year."
"Luck. This year I messed up the lay-ups because I'm useless under pressure. That won't change."
"You had a sprained wrist two weeks ago."
"That's an excuse. I'm being realistic."
"Realistic would be counting the wrist."
Chandrika pulled the blanket up to her chin. "You don't get it. If I try, I'll just fail again. Easier not to try."
Devika sat on the edge of the bed. "Then just come and watch the trials with me. No speaking."
"...Maybe."

qa.q: What happened to Chandrika's wrist two weeks ago?
qa.a: She had a sprained wrist two weeks ago.

qa.q: Why does Chandrika call her view "realistic"?
qa.a: She feels defeated and ashamed, and blaming herself feels like honesty, so the gloomy story seems true rather than a habit.

qa.q: How could Devika help Chandrika test her story?
qa.a: By naming real causes like the wrist and inviting a small, low-pressure step, like just watching the debate trials.

qa.q: What is it like for Devika to hear every fact dismissed?
qa.a: Devika may feel worried and frustrated, since each fact she offers gets turned into more proof against Chandrika.

grounding: Shows a teenager who blames herself for one setback, sees it as permanent and spreading to everything, and wants to give up while calling it realism.

passage:
Looking back at last term, I can see how fast I gave up. I'm Rajni, and when my chemistry practical went wrong, when the solution turned brown instead of blue, I decided it wasn't the practical. It was me. I'm careless, I thought. I've always been careless, and I'll be careless in the board exams too.
By Friday I'd left the quiz club and told Ankita not to put me in the history project group, because I'd drag everyone down. She said, "It was one test tube, Rajni." I told her I was just being honest.
It really felt like honesty then, not gloom. I still think some of it was true. But I also remember I hadn't slept the night before, and nobody in my batch got blue either.

qa.q: What colour did the solution turn in Rajni's practical?
qa.a: Brown instead of blue.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when leaving the quiz club?
qa.a: Rajni felt discouraged and ashamed, treating one failed practical as proof of being careless everywhere, for good.

qa.q: What facts could Rajni have checked before giving up?
qa.a: That there had been no sleep the night before and that nobody in the batch got blue, which point to a one-off, shared problem.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when told to leave Rajni out of the project?
qa.a: Ankita was probably worried and a little hurt, since one test tube didn't seem a reason to quit their group.

grounding: A teen looks back on blaming themselves for one failed practical, treating it as permanent and all-pervading, and quitting other things while it felt like realism.

passage:
Coach's log, Thursday. Devika, under-16 football.
Yusuf missed the second penalty in Saturday's semi-final. Since then he has skipped two practices. When I found him by the gate today, he said, "I always choke. I choked in the maths olympiad too. I'll choke in the boards. That's just me, coach." He said it flatly, like reading a weather report, not like someone upset. He believes this is honesty.
I reminded him he scored in the quarter-final and that the keeper guessed right on Saturday. He shrugged: "Lucky once."
Next steps: I asked him to come on Monday just to help set out cones, no shooting. I'll also speak with his class teacher, since he has handed in no homework this week.

qa.q: How many practices has Yusuf skipped since the semi-final?
qa.a: He has skipped two practices.

qa.q: What does Yusuf's flat voice suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems resigned and hopeless rather than openly upset, as if failing were a fixed fact about him.

qa.q: Why might asking Yusuf only to set out cones help?
qa.a: It keeps him connected to the team without the pressure of shooting, a small step that interrupts the habit of quitting.

qa.q: How does the coach read Yusuf's "That's just me"?
qa.a: Devika sees it as a learned habit of self-blame spreading to everything, not realism, and answers it with small steps and a word with his class teacher.

grounding: A coach's note shows a teenager treating one missed penalty as proof he always fails, spreading it to other areas and quitting while calling it honesty.

passage:
Thursday
Got 12 in the English test. Of course. I'm Varun, and this is just who I am: bad at English, bad at exams, bad at everything that matters.
Jyoti said, "It was one test. You got 17 last time." But she doesn't get it. Last time was luck. This is the real me.
I didn't go for football practice. What's the point? I'd probably mess that up too.
Mummy asked why I'm so quiet. I said nothing. I'm always going to be like this anyway.
I know Jyoti thinks I'm being dramatic. It doesn't feel dramatic. It feels true.

qa.q: What did Varun get in the last English test?
qa.a: Varun got 17 last time.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about the English test result?
qa.a: Varun feels hopeless and defeated, seeing the mark as proof of being bad at everything, forever.

qa.q: What could help Varun see the setback differently?
qa.a: Checking the evidence, like the 17 last time, and seeing one bad test as temporary and limited to English.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Varun's reaction?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as one test and thinks Varun is being dramatic, since the last mark was better.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees one setback as permanent and affecting everything, giving up quickly, and calling it realism.

passage:
In the village near Ludhiana, Amandeep's family's wheat crop was damaged by hail. He was sixteen and had been helping in the fields all year.
"Everything we do goes wrong," he said at dinner. "I'll fail my boards too. Why study?"
His friend Maria from the next farm came by the next day. "The hail hit our field too. It's the weather, not you."
"It's always us," Amandeep said. "Always."
He stopped going to evening tuition. He stopped playing kabaddi. He said he was just being realistic.
Maria sat on the wall of the tubewell. "Last year you topped the district science fair," she said. "Was that realistic too?"
Amandeep didn't answer.

qa.q: What damaged the wheat crop?
qa.a: Hail damaged the wheat crop.

qa.q: What is Amandeep feeling after the hail?
qa.a: He feels hopeless and defeated, sure that everything will always go wrong for him.

qa.q: How is Maria trying to help Amandeep?
qa.a: Maria points out that the hail hit their field too and that he topped the science fair, helping him see the setback as temporary and not his fault.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's family be affected by him giving up?
qa.a: They may feel worried about him, since he has stopped tuition and kabaddi when they need hope as well as help.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming himself for a setback, seeing it as permanent and affecting everything, and calling his giving up realism.

passage: Tomas didn't make the school band in Prague. Walking home, he laid out the case against himself. I'm bad at music. I'm bad at sports, too. I'm going to fail maths. Everything I try goes wrong, and it always will. He cancelled his guitar lesson that evening and put the case under the bed. Xin, who'd also auditioned and also missed out, messaged: "They only took two new people. I'll try again in spring. Want to practise together?" Tomas stared at the message. It seemed so simple for Xin. He typed, "What's the point," deleted it, typed it again. It felt like being realistic. It didn't occur to him that this was just one way of explaining one bad afternoon.

qa.q: How many new people did the band take?
qa.a: Only two new people.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling as he walked home?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and defeated, blaming himself and believing that everything he tries will always go wrong.

qa.q: What could Tomas say to himself instead of "What's the point"?
qa.a: That only two places were open and it was one audition, and that practising with Xin before spring could change the result.

qa.q: How does Xin see the same audition?
qa.a: Xin sees it as temporary and specific, a limited number of places, and plans to try again in spring.

grounding: Shows a teenager who blames himself for a setback, sees it as permanent and everywhere, and gives up quickly.

passage: At the football academy hostel, Asif missed a penalty in the inter-hostel final. That night, he didn't come down for dinner. "I always choke," he told Suraj, his roommate, staring at the ceiling. "In football, in exams, everywhere. I'm just that kind of person." The next morning, he skipped practice. The morning after, too. "Why bother? Coach will never trust me again." Suraj said, "Coach said it was a good strike, the keeper just guessed right." Asif shook his head. "You're being nice." To Asif, this felt like honesty, seeing himself clearly at last. Suraj went down to breakfast alone and, worried, mentioned it to the coach, who came up to the room that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Asif miss in the inter-hostel final?
qa.a: A penalty.

qa.q: How was Asif feeling while staring at the ceiling?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, convinced he always chokes and always will, everywhere.

qa.q: How could the coach help Asif see the miss differently?
qa.a: The coach could point to the good strike and the keeper's guess, and ask Asif back to practice to show one miss doesn't define him.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the missed penalty?
qa.a: Suraj sees it as bad luck, a good strike that the keeper guessed right, and is worried about his friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who explains a setback as permanent and all-pervasive and gives up quickly, believing it realism.

passage:
Charu,
You asked about the science test. I got 11 out of 40. That's it, I'm officially stupid. I've always been bad at science, and now it's spreading to everything. I'll probably fail maths next, then English, and then what? I stopped doing the revision sheets two days ago, what's the point. I know you'll say "it's just one test". But it doesn't feel like one test. It feels like finally seeing the truth. Mum says I'm being dramatic. Maybe. I just don't see how it changes. Remember last year when you told me I'm always hardest on myself? I keep thinking about that. I don't know if you're right.
Deepika

qa.q: What score did Deepika get in the science test?
qa.a: 11 out of 40.

qa.q: How is Deepika feeling about the test result?
qa.a: Deepika feels hopeless and defeated, convinced of being stupid and that the failure will spread to every subject.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepika about the revision sheets?
qa.a: Deepika could restart them for one topic missed in the test, testing whether the result is really permanent.

qa.q: How might Charu respond to this letter?
qa.a: Charu might gently remind Deepika that it is one test, not the whole truth, and that this harsh way of explaining setbacks is a habit.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees one bad result as permanent and all-pervasive and stops trying, feeling it is simple realism.

passage: Okay, Tejas, you asked why I didn't turn up for the second round of trials, so here it is. This Onam everyone's been at Ammachi's house, and I've been doing my usual thing: deciding I'm useless. I missed one header in the first round. One. And in my head it went: I'm slow, I'll always be slow, I'm slow at maths too, even my pookalam was the worst on the street this year. So why go back? I honestly thought I was just being realistic, you know? Then Ammachi found me sulking over my payasam and said, 'Jomon, you missed one ball, or you missed your whole life?' I laughed, but it stuck. With me it's never one bad thing. It's always everything, forever. Maybe that isn't the truth about me. Maybe it's just a habit I picked up somewhere, and habits can be unlearned.

qa.q: What happened to Jomon in the first round of the trials?
qa.a: Jomon missed one header.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after missing the header, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jomon felt defeated and useless: the one miss spread to maths and the pookalam too, and Jomon skipped the second round 😔

qa.q: What could Jomon ask the next time the 'I'm useless' story starts?
qa.a: Jomon could ask whether it was one miss or everything, whether it really lasts forever, and what one more try could change, just as Ammachi's question hinted.

qa.q: What might Ammachi have noticed while watching Jomon sulk over the payasam?
qa.a: Ammachi probably saw a grandchild blowing one missed ball up into a failed life, and her teasing question tried to shrink it back to its real size.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats one setback as permanent and about everything, gives up quickly, and mistakes this habit for realism.
